'''Sejong''' ({{Korean|hangul=세종|hanja=世宗}}; May 15, 1397 – April 8, 1450{{efn|Here, the birthday given in the [[Gregorian calendar]]. Most pre-1893 dates in this article use the [[Korean calendar]]; post-1893 dates will use the [[Gregorian calendar]]. Some pre-1893 dates have been converted to Gregorian because their anniversaries are of current interest.{{pb}}Korean calendar: 10th day, 4th month of 1397 – 17th day, 2nd month of 1450{{pb}}Julian calendar: May 7, 1397 – March 30, 1450}}), commonly known as '''Sejong the Great''' ({{korean|세종대왕|世宗大王||labels=no}}), was the fourth monarch of the Koreanic state [[Joseon]]. He ruled from 1418 to his death in 1450. He is widely regarded as the greatest king in Korean history, and is particularly remembered for the creation of [[Hangul]], the native alphabet of the [[Korean language]].

Sejong was born the third son of the future [[Taejong of Joseon|King Taejong]] ({{Reign|1400|1418}}). He was regarded as gifted, moreso than the troubled crown prince [[Grand Prince Yangnyŏng]]. In mid-1418, Yangnyŏng was deposed and Sejong made the crown prince. Months later, Taejong abdicated and Sejong was crowned king. Taejong served as [[T'aesangwang|king emeritus]] until his death in 1422.

Sejong's reign was marked by major developments in science, technology, medicine, agriculture, and the arts. Many such efforts Sejong not only oversaw, but actively participated in. In 1420, Sejong had the government research organization [[Hall of Worthies]] reestablished. It oversaw such projects as the creations of the first native Korean calendar {{ill|Ch'ilchŏngsan|ko|칠정산}}, the 365-volume medical text ''{{ill|Ŭibangyuch'wi|ko|의방유취}}'', and the agricultural text ''[[Nongsa chiksŏl]]''.

In 1419, Sejong launched the successful [[Ōei Invasion]] against the Japanese [[Tsushima Island]]. This was followed by decades of peace and trade between Korea and Japan. Sejong also expanded the northern borders of Korea to roughly its current extent by launching military campaigns against and assimilating the raiding [[Jurchen people|Jurchens]], although this region would remain problematic. He also maintained positive relations with Joseon's suzerain [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] while still asserting Korean autonomy. Sejong made significant tax and land reforms, which resulted in increases in agricultural production and a reduction in tax rates, without significant impact to tax income. He also led a massive expansion in the influence of [[Korean Confucianism|Confucianism in Korea]] and decrease in the influence of [[Korean Buddhism|Buddhism]]. Despite his anti-Buddhist policies, he was privately Buddhist and increasingly vocalized his faith, which put him at odds with the Confucianists of his court.

Sejong had recurring and worsening health issues for much of his life. Beginning in 1445, he had the crown prince, the future [[Munjong of Joseon|King Munjong]] ({{Reign|1450|1452}}), handle the daily affairs of government. Sejong died at the age of 52 in 1450 and is buried in the tomb [[Yeongneung]].

Sejong is regarded as an icon of [[Culture of Korea|Korean culture]] in South Korea, where he has received numerous tributes. [[Sejong City]] bears his name. Several North Korean texts reportedly skeptically evaluate Sejong as a feudal oppressor.

== Names and titles ==
{{Joseon monarchs}}

"Sejong" is the name by which he is most widely known.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=18}} It is a [[temple name]]: a posthumous title that was given to him on the 19th day, 3rd month of 1450.<ref name="Annals Temple">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1450 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:3월 19일에 존시를 영문 예무 인성 명효 대왕, 묘호를 세종이라고 올리다 |trans-chapter=On the 19th day of the 3rd month, granted the title Great King Yŏngmun Yemu Insŏng Myŏnghyo, temple name Sejong|chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_13202022_002}}</ref> Historian [[Gari Ledyard]] roughly translates its meaning as "epochal ancestor".{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=18}} Sejong's birth name was Yi To ({{Korean|hangul=이도|hanja=李祹|labels=no}}).{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=122}}<ref name="Annals Preface" /> In the 2nd month of 1408, Yi To was granted the name "Ch'ungnyŏng" ({{Korean|hangul=충녕|hanja=忠寧|labels=no}}) and the title "Prince" ({{Korean|hangul=군|hanja=君|labels=no}}).{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=122}}<ref name="Annals Preface" /> In the 5th month of 1413, Ch'ungnyŏng was granted the title "Grand Prince" ({{Korean|hangul=대군|hanja=大君|labels=no}}).{{Sfn|Hong|2004|p=9}}<ref name="Annals Preface" /> On the 27th day, 6th month of 1418, Ch'ungnyŏng was granted the [[courtesy name]] "Wŏnjŏng" ({{Korean|hangul=원정|hanja=元正|labels=no}}).<ref name="Annals Wonjong">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1431 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:왕세자의 자를 '원정'이라 하다 |trans-chapter=The Crown Prince receives the courtesy name 'Wŏnjŏng' |orig-year=1418 |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11806027_001}}</ref>

After his death, [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] granted him the title of Changhŏn ({{Korean|hangul=장헌|hanja=莊憲|labels=no}}; [[Pinyin]]: {{Transliteration|zh|pinyin|Zhuāngxiàn}}).{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=122}} His full posthumous title was Great King Changhŏn Yŏngmun Yemu Insŏng Myŏnghyo ({{Korean|hangul=장헌 영문 예무 인성 명효 대왕|hanja=莊憲英文睿武仁聖明孝大王|labels=no}}).<ref name="Annals Preface">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:총서 |trans-chapter=Preface |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_000}}</ref>

Sejong was reportedly popularly called the "Yao-Shun East of the Sea" ({{Korean/auto|hangul=^해동_^요순|hanja=海東堯舜|mr=yes|labels=no}}). The name references the legendary wise Chinese sage kings [[Emperor Yao|Yao]] and [[Emperor Shun|Shun]]. "East of the Sea" refers to Korea.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=190}}<ref name="Annals Death">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1450 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:임금이 영응 대군 집 동별궁에서 훙하다 |trans-chapter=His Majesty passes in the house of Grand Prince Yŏngŭng in the East Palace |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_13202017_001}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Yi To was born on the 10th day, 4th month of 1397 in Chunsubang,{{Efn|{{Korean|hangul=준수방|hanja=俊秀坊|labels=no}}. The exact location of Chunsubang is not known with certainty; it is believed to be outside of the current west gate [[Yeongchumun]] of the palace [[Gyeongbokgung]].{{sfn|Hong|2004|p=3}}}} [[Names of Seoul|Hanyang]] ([[Seoul]]), [[Joseon]] as the third son of father [[Taejong of Joseon|Grand Prince Chŏngan]] and [[Queen Wŏn'gyŏng|Princess Chŏngnyŏng]].{{Sfn|Hong|2004|p=3}}<ref name="Annals Preface" /> Yi To's father was the fifth son of the founding and reigning king of Joseon, [[Taejo of Joseon|Taejo]] ({{Reign|1392|1398}}).{{Sfn|Kang|2006a|p=194}}

Yi To was born five years after the founding of Joseon. His father, Grand Prince Chŏngan, had played a major role in the dynasty's establishment.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=8}} In 1398, Chŏngan became embroiled in a succession crisis.{{Sfn|Hong|2004|p=5}} He launched the {{Ill|First Strife of the Princes|ko|제1차 왕자의 난}}, which resulted in the installment of one of his brothers as [[Jeongjong of Joseon|King Jeongjong]] ({{Reign|1398|1400}}). After suppressing a coup in the {{ill|Second Strife of the Princes|ko|제2차 왕자의 난}}, Jeongjong abdicated the throne in favor of Chŏngan, who became King Taejong ({{Reign|1400|1418}}).{{Sfn|Kang|2006a|pp=194–195}}

Very little is known of Yi To's early life; few records were made of him, as it had seemed unlikely that he would ascend to the throne until just before he did.{{Sfn|Jung|2006|pp=134, 143}} One anecdote has it that the young Yi To read so much that his father became concerned for his health and took away his books; one book (the ''{{ill|Koso sugan|ko|구소수간}}'') that was missed Yi To read several times over.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=108–109|2a1=Jung|2y=2006|2pp=143–144|3a1=Volpe|3y=2023|3p=259}}<ref name="Annals Reading">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1423 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:임금이 《통감강목》의 강독에 대해 언급하다 |trans-chapter=His Majesty's comments on the reading of the T'onggam kangmok |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_10512023_001}}</ref><ref name="Annals Death" /> Several historians have evaluated this anecdote as possibly fanciful,{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=108–109|2a1=Volpe|2y=2023|2pp=261–262}} but Ledyard argued it was plausible given Yi To's lifelong academic interests.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=108–109}} In 1413, Taejong told Yi To (who by then was called Ch'ungnyŏng): "you have nothing to do in particular, so you should just enjoy your life in peace".{{efn|{{lang|ko|너는 할 일이 없으니, 평안하게 즐기기나 할 뿐이다}}; {{lang|ko|汝無所事, 安享而已}}}} At this point, Ch'ungnyŏng was already considered to be bright and skilled at the arts, including calligraphy, the [[Gayageum|''gayageum'']] (traditional Korean string instrument), and painting.{{sfn|Kang|2006b|p=75}}<ref name="Annals Enjoy">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1413 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:세자와 제 대군과 공주가 헌수하고 노래와 시를 올리다 |trans-chapter=The crown prince, grand prince, and princess made offerings, sang songs, and read poetry |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11312030_003}}</ref> That year, he began to be tutored by scholar-official {{ill|Yi Su|ko|이수 (문정공)}}.{{Sfn|Jung|2006|pp=143–144}}

=== Heir to the throne ===
By 1406, Taejong had decided that he wished to eventually abdicate the throne to a successor while he was still alive, to reduce the probability of a succession crisis upon his death.{{Sfn|Hong|2004|p=8}} Taejong had twelve sons, the oldest of which was [[Grand Prince Yangnyŏng]]. Yangnyŏng was designated the successor.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=8}}

A number of anecdotes indicate that Yangnyŏng was considered to have behavioral issues.{{sfnm|1a1=Hong|1y=2004|1pp=6–10|2a1=Kim|2y=2014|2pp=417–418}}<ref name="Annals Deposed">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1431 |language=Korean |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |script-chapter=ko:세자 이제를 폐하고 충녕 대군으로서 왕세자를 삼다 |trans-chapter=Yangnyŏng is deposed and Ch'ungnyŏng becomes heir apparent |orig-year=1418 |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11806003_001}}</ref> Yangnyŏng disobeyed the king frequently, neglected studying, and womanized.{{Sfn|Hong|2004|pp=6–10}} Taejong strictly and sternly managed Yangnyŏng's education. Historian Kim Young Soo argued that this may have pushed Yangnyŏng away from studying.{{Sfn|Kim|2014|pp=418–419}} The king also disliked the companions of the grand prince; on several occasions they were banned from the palace for their behavior.{{Sfn|Hong|2004|pp=6–10}} By contrast, various anecdotes in the ''{{ill|Veritable Records of Taejong|ko|태종실록}}'' indicate that Ch'ungnyŏng was seen as intelligent and studious by the king and various members of the court. The king frequently praised Ch'ungnyŏng and compared him favorably to Yangnyŏng, to the latter's chagrin. On several occasions, Ch'ungnyŏng chastised the misbehavior of Yangnyŏng, which only fueled the latter's resentment, although on several occasions Yangnyŏng acknowledged his brother's better judgement. The two developed a bitter rivalry.{{sfnm|1a1=Jung|1y=2006|1pp=144–146|2a1=Kim|2y=2014|2pp=417–418, 423–424}}

In early 1417, it emerged that Yangnyŏng had had an affair with a woman named Ŏri ({{Korean|hangul=어리|hanja=於里|labels=no}}), a concubine of scholar-official [[Kwak Sŏn]] ({{Korean|hangul=곽선|hanja=郭璇|labels=no}}). The incident enraged and embarrassed Taejong.{{sfn|Kim|2014|p=426}}<ref name="Annals Ori">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1417 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:세자가 곽선의 첩 어리를 간통하여 궁중에 들여온 사건 기사 |trans-chapter=Record of the crown prince bringing Ŏri, wife of Kwak Sŏn, into the palace to have an affair |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11702015_002}}</ref> Yangnyŏng angrily accused Ch'ungnyŏng of having informed their father of the affair.{{sfn|Kim|2014|p=424}}

In early 1418, the younger brother of Ch'ungnyŏng, {{ill|Grand Prince Sŏngnyŏng|ko|성녕대군}}, was deathly ill.{{sfn|Kim|2014|pp=426–427}} Ch'ungnyŏng reportedly stayed by his brother's bed day and night, reading medical texts and helping with the treatment.{{Sfn|Jung|2006|p=145}}<ref name="Annals Brother">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1418 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:성녕 대군 이종의 졸기 |trans-chapter=Passing of Grand Prince Sŏngnyŏng Yi Chong |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11802004_001}}</ref> Sŏngnyŏng died on the 4th day, 2nd month of that year.{{Sfn|Yoon|2013|p=112}}<ref name="Annals Brother" /> Afterwards, Taejong went to [[Kaesong]] and nominally left Yangnyŏng in charge of the capital in his absence. He quietly ordered that Yangnyŏng be functionally isolated and monitored; he wished to see if Yangnyŏng would change his ways.{{Sfn|Yoon|2013|pp=117–121}} In his father's absence, Yangnyŏng brought Ŏri back into the palace, where she gave birth to their child. When Taejong learned of this, he wept and confided to several ministers that he had little faith in Yangnyŏng's ability to govern.{{Sfn|Kim|2014|pp=426–427}}<ref name="Annals Ori2">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |language=Korean |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |script-chapter=ko:임금이 조말생에게 세자의 불의를 말하다 |trans-chapter=His Majesty informs Cho Malsaeng about the crown prince's injustices |year=1418 |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11803006_002}}</ref> Historian Yoon Jeong argues that, around this time, Taejong worked on building consensus among his cabinet to have Yangnyŏng removed from his position.{{Sfn|Yoon|2013|pp=121–124}} Their relationship reached its lowest point in the 5th month of that year, after Yangnyŏng sent a letter to his father in which he defended his actions and questioned his father's judgment.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2014|1p=428|2a1=Yoon|2y=2013|2p=124}}<ref name="Annals Ori3">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |language=Korean |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |script-chapter=ko:세자가 내관 박지생을 보내어 친히 지은 수서를 상서하다 |trans-chapter=The crown prince has eunuch Pak Chisaeng deliver a letter he had written |year=1418 |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kca_11805030_001}}</ref>

On the 3rd day, 6th month of 1418, Taejong and his ministers held a meeting on whether to depose Yangnyŏng.{{efn|According to the ''[[Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty]]'', it was the court that petitioned Taejong to hold this meeting.<ref name="Annals Deposed" /> Historians have instead argued that Taejong was the driving force behind the meeting.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2014|1pp=428–429|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1990|2p=8|3a1=Yoon|3y=2013|3pp=125–126}} Ledyard argued that Taejong held this meeting just months before his abdication in order to surprise potential opposers.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=8}}}}{{Sfn|Hong|2004|pp=11–12}}<ref name="Annals Deposed" /> The topic was contentious as it required overriding the stable practice of [[primogeniture]].{{sfn|Kim|2014|p=430}} Despite some opposition from the queen and several in the court, it was decided that Yangnyŏng would be demoted and exiled to [[Gwangju]]. It was also decided that they would select the new successor based on their merits. Taejong described his second son, [[Grand Prince Hyoryŏng]], as weak and overly agreeable. He then nominated Ch'ungnyŏng, whom he praised as studious and wise. The court reportedly enthusiastically agreed with Taejong's nomination.{{Sfn|Hong|2004|pp=11–12}}<ref name="Annals Deposed" /> There is an anecdote that these decisions weighed heavily on Taejong, and that he wept after making them.{{sfnm|1a1=Hong|1y=2004|1pp=11–12|2a1=Kim|2y=2014|2p=429}} Yangnyŏng took the news of his deposal calmly and quickly became detached from politics. Kim argued that Yangnyŏng had likely anticipated this happening. He was eventually invited back to the capital by his brother and the two got along well.{{Sfn|Kim|2014|pp=429–436}}

A number of historians have argued that Sejong's successful reign was made possible by the stability created by Taejong's competent statecraft.{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1p=228|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1990|2pp=8–9|3a1=Park|3y=2018|3p=9}}<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Kim |first=Djun Kil |title=The History of Korea |publisher=[[Greenwood Press]] |year=2005a |isbn=0-313-33296-7 |edition=1st |pages=74–77 |url=https://archive.org/details/historyofkorea0000kimc/mode/2up |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> Historian Djun Kil Kim argued that Sejong also benefitted from being surrounded by experienced military officials that had worked under his father.<ref name=":7" /> By the time that Sejong took the throne, bureaucratic institutions had been in place for around 15 years.{{Sfn|Duncan|2000|p=136}}
[[File:Sujeongjeon.JPG|thumb|During Sejong's reign, the building [[Sujeongjeon]] in Gyeongbokgung hosted the [[Hall of Worthies]]<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |author=김동현 |script-title=ko:경복궁 수정전 (景福宮 修政殿) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0002446 |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>]]
In 1420, Sejong designed and reestablished the [[Hall of Worthies]].{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1pp=228–229|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2p=91|3a1=Pratt|3y=2007|3p=120}} Modern historians have likened the institution to a [[think tank]];{{sfnm|1a1=Jin|1y=2005|1p=392|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1990|2p=9|3a1=Grayson|3y=2002|3p=109}} it oversaw major cultural and intellectual pursuits, especially for issues of governance, as well as the education of the king and crown prince.{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1pp=228–229|2a1=Jin|2y=2005|2p=392}} In 1426, he ordered that the institution began a practice called ''{{ill|saga toksŏ|ko|사가독서}}'': allowing scholars to independently research without participating in government work;{{sfnm|1a1=Volpe|1y=2023|1pp=267–268|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2p=91|3a1=Jin|3y=2005|3p=392|4a1=Oh|4y=2013|4p=213}} this has been likened to modern research grants.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=91|2a1=Oh|2y=2013|2p=213}}

In 1421, Sejong made Gyeongbokgung his primary palace.{{Sfn|이강근|2007|pp=36–37}} In 1426, he had many major gates and bridges of the palace named.{{Sfn|이강근|2007|p=37}} By 1427, he officially moved out of the secondary palace [[Changdeokgung]] and into Gyeongbokgung,{{Sfn|이강근|2007|pp=36–37}} although he would continue to move between the two often.<ref>{{Cite book |author=임석재 |url=https://play.google.com/store/books/details/%EC%9E%84%EC%84%9D%EC%9E%AC_%EC%98%88_%EF%A6%B6_%EB%A1%9C_%EC%A7%80%EC%9D%80_%EA%B2%BD%EB%B3%B5%EA%B6%81?id=8MHEDwAAQBAJ |title=예(禮)로 지은 경복궁: 동양 미학으로 읽다 |date=2019-12-10 |publisher=인물과사상사 |isbn=978-89-5906-551-6 |pages=82 |language=ko |trans-title=Gyeongbokgung, Built with Conscientiousness: An Eastern Art Perspective}}</ref> Sejong greatly renovated and expanded the palace.{{Sfn|이강근|2007|pp=36–37}} It was during Sejong's reign that Gyeongbokgung became fully-fledged and functional; it would remain in much the same state from his reign for around a hundred years afterwards.{{Sfn|이강근|2007|pp=36–39}}

== Science, mathematics, and technology ==
Sejong oversaw one of the most productive eras in Korean science.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=1998|1pp=56–57|2a1=Jeon|2y=2011|2p=395}} Several historians have described his reign as a "golden age" for the field.{{sfnm|1a1=Jeon|1y=2011|1p=395|2a1=Kim|2y=2019|2p=136}}

=== Astronomy, meteorology, calendars, and timekeeping ===
[[File:BoRuGak Jagyeongnu.JPG|thumb|Part of the water clock [[Borugak Jagyeongnu]]. Built during Sejong's reign, when it rang the time would be relayed to the rest of the city.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=박성래 |script-title=ko:보루각 (報漏閣) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0023286 |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>]]
Sejong oversaw significant research into [[astronomy]].{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=90}} In 1432, a [[solar eclipse]] occurred two days later than predicted; this motivated Sejong to commission the research and development of [[List of astronomical instruments|astronomical instruments]] such as globes, [[Planisphere|planispheres]], and sun dials.{{Sfn|Wang|2023|pp=69–70}} An [[armillary sphere]] was created in 1433.{{Sfn|Jeon|2011|p=121}} A [[water clock]] was designed by Chang Yŏngsil in 1434.{{Sfn|Jeon|2011|p=32}} In 1434{{sfnm|1a1=Jeon|1y=2011|1pp=78–79|2a1=Lee|2y=1984|2p=196}} or 1438,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nam |first1=Moon-hyon |chapter=Highlights of King Sejong's Astronomical Project: Observatory Ganui-dae and Calendar Chiljeong-san |date=2015 |title=A Bridge between Conceptual Frameworks: Sciences, Society and Technology Studies |pages=324 |editor-last=Pisano |editor-first=Raffaele |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-9645-3_17 |access-date=2025-07-25 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-9645-3_17 |isbn=978-94-017-9645-3 |last2=Nha |first2=Il–seong}}</ref> the observatory {{Ill|Ganuidae|ko|간의대}} was established in Gyeongbokgung by order of Sejong.{{Sfn|이강근|2007|p=37}} In 1441, Prince Yi Hyang (the future [[Munjong of Joseon|King Munjong]]) led Korean scientists {{ill|Yi Ch'ŏn|ko|이천 (1376년)}} and Chang Yŏngsil in inventing the [[Ch'ŭgugi|''ch'ŭgugi'']]:{{sfnm|1a1=Lim|1y=2019|1pp=194–195|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=214}} a [[rain gauge]], the likes of which would not be invented in Europe until [[Benedetto Castelli]]'s invention in 1639.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=214}} In 1442, ''ch'ŭgugi'' were distributed around Joseon.{{sfnm|1a1=Lim|1y=2019|1pp=194–195|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2p=90|3a1=Park|3y=2022|3p=164|4a1=Seth|4y=2010|4p=184}} They fell out of use in the late 16th century, but were brought back in 1770 and saw continued use until the end of the Joseon period.{{Sfn|Lim|2019|pp=196–197}} The ''[[sup'yo]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=수표|hanja=水標|labels=no}}), a [[stream gauge]], was invented in 1442.{{Sfn|Jeon|2011|pp=28–29, 143–144}}

Under Sejong, Korea began to develop its own indigenous calendar tradition for the first time. Prior to Sejong's reign, Korea was not able to accurately calculate dates or the positions of major heavenly bodies; it instead relied on calculations and [[Chinese calendar|calendars from China]]. These calculations were dependent on China's position on the Earth and were thus ill-suited for use in Korea. The use of Chinese calendars was in part political; it was seen as obligatory for Joseon to defer to the use of the calendar of its suzerain, Ming.{{sfnm|1a1=Moon|1y=2019|1pp=258–259, 264–266|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2p=90|3a1=Park|3y=2022|3p=164}} In addition, Ming guarded the calculation methods for their calendar systems.{{Sfn|Wang|2023|pp=69–70}} In 1433, studies on calendar systems from China and elsewhere were launched.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=90}} Sejong ordered that such studies be kept secret from Ming.{{Sfn|Wang|2023|p=70}} In 1444, Sejong's court devised a new calendar: "{{ill|Ch'ilchŏngsan|ko|칠정산}}".{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=215|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2p=164|3a1=Park|3y=2019|3p=140}} It used Seoul as its reference point.{{sfnm|1a1=Park|1y=2022|1p=164|2a1=Wang|2y=2023|2p=70}} It allowed them to accurately predict lunar and solar eclipses in 1447.{{Sfn|Kim|1998|p=57}} It was revised beginning in 1448, due to inconsistencies with the Chinese calendar. Historian Park Kwon Soo argued the inconsistencies were not mistakes, and were instead merely due to the differing locations of Beijing and Seoul. Nevertheless, Sinocentric Korean scholars expressed concerns about departing from Chinese calculations.{{sfn|Park|2019|pp=140–141}}

=== Medicine ===
Sejong also oversaw significant advances in Korean medicine. Historian of Korean medicine Kim Dujong argued that Sejong created "the foundation of medicine in Joseon".{{Sfn|Kim|2019|p=136}} Sejong attempted to systematize both medical research and practice, with the latter grounded in the former.{{Sfn|Kim|2019|p=137}} Historians Tae-jin Yi and Sang-Woon Jeon argue that innovations in medicine in Sejong's reign contributed to a multiplying of population growth between the 13th and 15th centuries.{{Sfn|Yi|Jeon|Baker|1992|p=98}}

Sejong took personal interest in medical education. In 1421, he had the medical school [[Ŭisŏ sŭptokkwan]] ({{Korean|hangul=의서습독관|hanja=醫書習讀官|labels=no}}) established.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Hun Pyeng |last2=Oh |first2=Junho |date=December 2018 |title=15-16세기 조선 의학 관료의 신분 변천: 양성이씨 세전 사례를 중심으로 |trans-title=The Change of the Status of Joseon Medical Bureaucrats in the 15th and 16th Centuries |journal=Korean Journal of Medical History |language=ko |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=299–300 |doi=10.13081/kjmh.2018.27.295 |issn=1225-505X |pmc=10565050 |pmid=30679408 }}</ref> In 1427, he ordered that medical students be given support so that they can focus on their studies.{{Sfn|Kim|2019|p=141}}<ref name="Annals Students">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1427 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:매년말 지방 감사가 의원 생도 2, 3인을 뽑아 전의감과 혜민국에 보내게 하다 |trans-chapter=At the end of each year, local auditors are to select two to three medical students and send them to the Chŏnŭigam and Hyemin'guk |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_10911002_006}}</ref> In 1430, he ordered that the ''{{ill|ŭigwa|ko|의과 (과거제)}}'' (medical examination) be reformed; major texts on [[traditional Chinese medicine]] and even veterinarian studies were added to the curriculum.{{Sfn|Kim|2019|pp=142–143}}<ref name="Annals Uigwa">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1430 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:상정소에서 여러 학의 취재에 있어 경서와 여러 기예의 수목에 대하여 아뢰다 |trans-chapter=Sangjŏngso report on the various works on various subjects used for examinations |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_11203018_002}}</ref>
[[File:의방유취 (醫方類聚).jpg|thumb|Cover of a volume of ''{{ill|Ŭibangyuch'wi|ko|의방유취}}'']]
In 1433, the 56-volume medical text ''{{ill|Hyangyakchipsŏngbang|ko|향약집성방}}'' was compiled.{{sfnm|1a1=Pratt|1y=2007|1p=121|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2p=165|3a1=Kim|3y=2012|3p=215|4a1=Kim|4y=2019|4pp=149–151}} It became a major medical text; it was intended to serve as a comprehensive medical guide and was multiple times larger than its predecessor ''{{ill|Hyangyak chesaeng chipsŏngbang|ko|향약제생집성방}}''. It described hundreds of symptoms and over 10,000 treatments.{{Sfn|Kim|2019|pp=149–151}} The work was based on research on traditional medicine throughout Korea, and included comparisons to Chinese medicine. It became a prized source of information in Ming as well.{{Sfn|Wells|2015|p=83}} In 1445 or 1447,{{Efn|The 1445 first attestation to the text in the ''Veritable Records'' is unclear about when the ''Ŭibang yuchwi'' was completed. It both says that the text was commissioned and that it was completed on that date after three years of work.{{sfn|Kim|2019|pp=154–155}} Historian Kim Seongsu argued that it was completed by 1447.{{sfn|Kim|2019|pp=154–155}}}} the 365-volume medical text ''{{ill|Ŭibangyuch'wi|ko|의방유취}}'' was completed.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=90|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2p=165|3a1=Kim|3y=2019|3pp=153–155}}<ref name="Annals Uibangyuchwi">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1445 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:《의방유취》가 완성되다 |trans-chapter=Ŭibangyuch'wi is completed |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12710027_002}}</ref> Medical historian Kim Seongsu argues the text's scale dwarfs that of contemporary Chinese medical texts, and that it was possibly among the largest research projects in East Asia at the time. Kim also argued that this text may have also been applied to Sejong's treatment, as Sejong ordered that it be consulted months before he died.{{sfn|Kim|2019|p=157}}

In 1443, he ordered that the palace pharmacy Naeyakbang ({{Korean|hangul=내약방|hanja=內藥房|labels=no}}) be reorganized into the royal medical agency [[Naeŭiwŏn]].{{Sfn|Kim|2019|pp=139–140}}<ref name="Annals Naeyakbang">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1443 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:내약방의 이름과 관원의 호칭 등을 정하다 |trans-chapter=Names of the Naeyakbang and its officials are chosen |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12506015_002}}</ref> Sejong also made efforts to lower the cost of medicine. He implemented price controls, established a fund that subsidized more expensive medicines, and attempted to substitute expensive foreign ingredients for domestic. In 1423 and 1430, he had Korean medical researchers visit China and work with Chinese researchers to determine what native Korean ingredients could serve as adequate substitutes for Chinese ingredients. This research resulted in the creation of the 1431 medical text ''[[Hyangyak ch'aech'wi wŏllyŏng]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=향약채취월령|hanja=鄕藥採取月令|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0062962 |access-date=2025-07-29 |language=ko |author=남풍현 |script-title=ko:향약채취월령 (鄕藥採取月令)}}</ref>).{{Sfn|Kim|2019|pp=143–147}} 

=== Movable type ===
[[File:갑인자 (3).JPG|thumb|[[Kabin type|''Kabin'' types]] set on a plate]]
Sejong's reign was a high point in innovations in Korean [[movable type]] technology.{{sfnm|1a1=Oh|1y=2013|1p=106|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=216|3a1=Jeon|3y=2011|3pp=28–29}} In 1420, Sejong ordered the casting of new [[Kyŏngja type|''kyŏngja'' types]] ({{Korean|hangul=경자자|hanja=庚子字|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=천혜봉 |script-title=ko:경자자 (庚子字) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0002757 |access-date=2025-07-24 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>). The previously used [[Kyemi type|''kyemi'' types]] ({{Korean|hangul=계미자|hanja=癸未字|labels=no}}) required the use of adhesive [[beeswax]] to [[Typesetting|secure type to plate]]; this process was laborious and slow. The ''kyŏngja'' types instead relied on faster mechanical methods of typesetting, and allowed multiple times more pages to be printed per day.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=216|2a1=Oh|2y=2013|2p=107|3a1=Sohn|3y=1992|3p=53|4a1=Lee|4y=1984|4pp=196–197}} In 1434, Sejong's court cast a set of more than 200,000 [[Kabin type|''kabin'' types]] ({{Korean|hangul=갑인자|hanja=甲寅字|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=천혜봉 |script-title=ko:갑인자 (甲寅字) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0000932 |access-date=2025-07-24 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>) that were made of copper.{{sfnm|1a1=Park|1y=2022|1p=165|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=216|3a1=Jeon|3y=2011|3pp=272–273|4a1=Oh|4y=2013|4p=107|5a1=Wells|5y=2015|5p=80}} The ''kabin'' types were as twice as efficient to use as ''kyŏngja'' types.{{sfnm|1a1=Oh|1y=2013|1p=108|2a1=Wells|2y=2015|2p=80}} ''Kabin'' type were manufactured five,{{Sfn|Jeon|2011|p=277}} six,{{Sfn|Wells|2015|p=80}} or seven{{Sfn|Sohn|1992|p=53}} additional times in the future. After 1437, lead types began to be used.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=216}} The use of such types was also regulated. Punishments were established for mistakes and poor worksmanship.{{Sfn|Sohn|1992|p=56}}

=== Agriculture ===
[[File:農事直說 농사직설.jpg|thumb|Cover of a copy of ''[[Nongsa chiksŏl]]'']]
Sejong oversaw a notable increase in agricultural productivity.{{sfnm|1a1=Song et al.|1y=2019|1pp=158–161|2a1=Yi|2a2=Jeon|2a3=Baker|2y=1992|2p=99}} In 1429, the agricultural treatise ''[[Nongsa chiksŏl]]'' was completed under order of Sejong.{{sfnm|1a1=Pratt|1y=2007|1p=121|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2pp=213–214|3a1=Jeon|3y=2011|3pp=37–38}} The work was meant to be more directly suited to Korean agriculture than Chinese works.{{Sfn|Lee|1984|p=195}} The text contains anecdotes from experienced farmers around Korea and remained a foundational work in Korean agriculture studies until the 17th century.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=214}} It contributed to a multiplication of agricultural output by the end of the reign of [[Seongjong of Joseon|King Seongjong]] ({{reign|1469|1494}}).{{sfn|Song et al.|2019|p=158}} Sejong took personal charge of an experiment on palace land on crop management in bad weather.{{Sfn|Pratt|2007|p=121}} Advancements in irrigation and the [[sericulture]] were also made.{{Sfn|Pratt|2007|pp=120–121}} Innovations in other fields during Sejong's reign, including the development of rain gauges, more accurate calendars, and tax reform, also contributed to agriculture.{{Sfn|Yi|Jeon|Baker|1992|pp=99–101}} 

=== Mathematics ===
Sejong was a significant advocate for the study and use of mathematics in Joseon.{{sfn|Wells|2015|p=81}} At the time, mathematics was seen as a field for lower-level bureaucrats and not Confucian scholars, especially not rulers. Sejong went against this social norm by studying mathematics himself.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=109–110, 120}} Sejong said of mathematics:

{{Blockquote|text=It is said that mathematics is nothing more than a mechanical skill, but it is indispensable to the administration of the state. But for the participation of {{ill|Yi Sunji|ko|이순지}}, [[Kim Tam]] and others in the recent [[cadastre|cadastral]] survey, it is questionable the land could have been measured properly. By all means devise measures to ensure the maximum development of mathematics throughout the land.{{sfn|Wells|2015|p=81}}<ref name="Annals Mathematics">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1443 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:산학을 예습하게 할 방책을 세우려 집현전으로 하여금 역대 산학의 법을 상고하게 하다 |trans-chapter=Order that the Hall of Worthies study historical texts on arithmetic in order to establish an arithmetic curriculum |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12511017_003}}</ref>|title=''Veritable Records of Sejong'', 17th day, 11th month of 1443}}

In 1431, Sejong sent promising mathematicians to China for study. In 1433, a 100-volume treatise on mathematics was printed, and in 1438 five mathematics texts were added to curriculums of technical colleges; afterwards mathematics became around half their curriculum. Unlike under some other monarchs when mathematics was neglected, Sejong encouraged the use of mathematics in government; people skilled in math were employed to administer taxes, take the census, and manage currency and accounting.{{Sfn|Wells|2015|pp=81–82}}

=== Cartography ===
Sejong's administration also made advances in [[cartography]]. In 1424, Sejong ordered that a national geography be compiled.{{Sfn|Lewis|2003|p=225}} In 1432 or 1434,{{efn|Jinwung Kim and James B. Lewis claim the maps were completed in 1432.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=213|2a1=Lewis|2y=2003|2p=225}} Ledyard claims that the maps were completed in 1434 after surveys were completed in 1432.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=89}}}} a collection of maps of Korea called "Sinch'an p'alto chiriji" ({{Korean|신찬팔도지리지|新撰八道地理志|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |script-title=ko:신찬팔도지리지 (新撰八道地理志) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0033423 |access-date=2025-07-24 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>) was prepared based on records and surveying efforts.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=89|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=213}} This work was eventually incorporated into a 1454 larger collection of maps called "{{ill|Sejong sillok chiriji|ko|세종실록 지리지}}".{{Efn|The work so named because it was appended to the ''Veritable Records of Sejong'' (''Sejong sillok'').{{sfn|Kim|2012|p=213}}}}{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=213}} These maps served as foundation and reference for later maps and works.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=10}}

=== Weaponry ===
[[File:Korean rocket arrows.jpg|thumb|''[[Sin'gijŏn]]'' of various sizes]]
Sejong commissioned the 1448 text ''[[Ch'ongt'ong tŭngnok]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=총통등록|hanja=銃筒騰錄|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=전상운 |script-title=ko:총통등록 (銃筒騰錄) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0057157 |access-date=2025-07-24 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>), which covered the manufacture and deployment of firearms.{{sfnm|1a1=Park|1y=2022|1p=165|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=215|3a1=Jeon|3y=2011|3p=35|4a1=Lee|4y=1984|4p=197}} ''[[Sin'gijŏn]]'' (fire arrow rockets) were developed and first attested to in 1448, during Sejong's reign.{{Sfn|Korea Foundation|2011|p=109}}

== Arts and culture ==

=== Music ===
[[File:Encykorea-악장가사 여민락.jpg|thumb|The lyrics of the song [[Yŏmillak]], which was composed by Sejong himself]]
Sejong and his administration had a major influence in [[Korean court music]]. Sejong observed the ''[[aak]]'' genre music of the Korean court and felt that it had degenerated from ancient Chinese ideals. He and several scholars consulted Chinese texts and attempted to rejuvenate Korean practice.{{sfnm|1a1=Saeji|1y=2025|1pp=325–326|2a1=Provine|2y=1992|2p=74}}

From 1420 to 1425, Sejong had new court music produced.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=99}} From 1423 to 1430, Sejong's chief musicologist [[Pak Yŏn]] oversaw the creations of hundreds of court music instruments.{{Sfn|Provine|1992|p=74}} In 1430, after consulting ancient Chinese musicology texts, Sejong ordered that Pak Yŏn, Chŏng Inji, and others develop new music for Confucian rites. These efforts resulted in the recreations of several ancient Chinese instruments and a musical treatise that would be appended to the ''Veritable Records of Sejong''.{{sfnm|1a1=Provine|1y=1974|1pp=2–3, 13–14|2a1=Provine|2y=1992|2pp=75–76}} Reforms on court music continued, with new songs performed in 1433.{{sfnm|1a1=Pratt|1y=2007|1pp=121, 124|2a1=Provine|2y=1992|2p=76}} Under Sejong's reign, the first [[mensural notation]] scheme in Asia was developed.{{sfnm|1a1=Saeji|1y=2025|1pp=325–326|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2p=166}}

Beginning in 1433, focus shifted away from the emulation of Chinese practice to the development of native Korean practice. That year, he called for [[Traditional music of Korea|folk music]] from around Korea be gathered, although it is unknown if this project was completed.{{Sfn|Provine|1992|pp=76–77}}

Research conducted on Chinese musicology in Sejong's reign was eventually compiled into the 1493 text ''[[Akhak kwebŏm]]''.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=93|2a1=Pratt|2y=2007|2pp=121, 124|3a1=Lee|3a2=Ramsey|3y=2011|3pp=243–244}} This work has been evaluated as an extremely valuable source of information on traditional Sino-Korean music.{{sfnm|1a1=Pratt|1y=2007|1pp=121, 124|2a1=Grayson|2y=2002|2p=110}}

Sejong composed music himself. He composed [[Yŏmillak]].{{Sfn|Park|2022|p=166}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0036342 |access-date=2025-07-24 |language=ko |author=한명희 |script-title=ko:여민락 (與民樂)}}</ref> In 1447, he created the pieces [[Pot'aep'yŏng]] ({{Korean|hangul=보태평|hanja=保太平|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0023574 |access-date=2025-07-22 |language=ko |author=문숙희 |script-title=ko:보태평 (保太平)}}</ref>) and [[Chŏngdaeŏp]] ({{Korean|hangul=정대업|hanja=定大業|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0050072 |access-date=2025-07-22 |language=ko |author=장사훈 |script-title=ko:정대업 (定大業)}}</ref>).{{sfnm|1a1=Provine|1y=1992|1p=77|2a1=Saeji|2y=2025|2pp=325–326}} These two pieces were adapted and continued to be performed until the end of the Joseon period.{{Sfn|Provine|1992|p=78}} He also composed the music for the 1449 Buddhist text ''[[Sari yŏngŭnggi]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=사리영응기|hanja=舍利靈應記|labels=no}}).{{Sfn|Pu|2005|pp=28–29}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=강호선 |script-title=ko:사리영응기 (舍利靈應記) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0025548 |access-date=2025-07-30 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>

=== Ceremonial rites ===
In the practice of ceremonial rites, Sejong attempted to preserve Korean tradition while also introducing ancient Chinese tradition.{{sfnm|1a1=Deuchler|1y=1992|1p=123|2a1=Pratt|2y=2007|2p=121}} In 1444, Sejong ordered that research on the {{ill|Five Rites (Joseon)|lt=Five Rites|ko|오례}} be completed. Historian [[Martina Deuchler]] argued that it is clear Sejong supervised the compilation and gave his own input. Once completed in 1451, a copy of the work was appended to the ''Veritable Records of Sejong''.{{Sfn|Deuchler|1992|pp=118–119}}

=== Art and calligraphy ===
[[File:Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land.jpg|thumb|The landmark painting ''{{ill|Mongyudowŏndo|ko|몽유도원도}}'' was produced during Sejong's reign]]
Sejong's reign is considered a high point in the history of Korean painting.{{sfn|Ahn|1992|p=81}} Significant quantities of art were sponsored and produced during this period. Major artists of this period include [[Southern School|literati painter]] [[Kang Hŭian]], {{ill|Ch'oe Kyŏng|ko|최경}}, {{ill|Yi Sangjwa|ko|이상좌}}, and [[An Kyŏn]].{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=217|2a1=Nahm|2y=1996|2p=115|3a1=Ahn|3y=1992|3p=81}} In 1447, An produced the landmark painting ''{{ill|Mongyudowŏndo|ko|몽유도원도}}'', which is said to be based on a dream of Sejong's third son {{ill|Grand Prince Anp'yŏng|ko|안평대군}}. Calligraphy also florished; that grand prince was himself a renowned calligrapher.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=217|2a1=Lee|2y=1984|2pp=197–198}}

=== Literature ===
Sejong has been described as a "[[Bookworm|bibliophile]]".{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=108–109|2a1=Pratt|2y=2007|2p=121}} Anecdotes indicate that Sejong enjoyed reading as well as the collection and preservation of rare books.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=108–109|2a1=Pu|2y=2005|2p=29|3a1=Jung|3y=2006|3p=144|4a1=Volpe|4y=2023|4pp=259–261}} In 1442, he ordered governors in the southern provinces to gather information on his father's past exploits in suppressing Japanese pirates; these stories were developed into the work ''[[Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga]]''.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=327–329, 370}} That work then became the first major piece of literature in Hangul, after its Korean poems were completed around 1447.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=327–329, 370|2a1=Volpe|2y=2025|2pp=63–64|3a1=Kim|3y=2007|3p=147}}

== Domestic policy ==
Sejong attempted to govern primarily by Confucian principles.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1990|1p=17|2a1=Yoo|2y=2006|2pp=10–11}} According to historian Christopher Lovins, Sejong's reign is widely viewed as the "full flowering of Confucianism in Korea".{{Sfn|Lovins|2019|p=277}}

Sejong believed that deliberation was important to good governance.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=61–62}} Although Sejong was one of the most powerful Joseon monarchs, he and other Joseon monarchs were generally strongly checked by the high bureaucracy.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=112–113|2a1=Jin|2y=2005|2pp=392–393|3a1=Jin|3y=2005|3pp=388–389, 394}} Several historians have evaluated Sejong as open, in part intentionally, to vigorous debate and even criticism.{{sfnm|1a1=Park|1y=2005|1pp=61–62|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1990|2pp=7–8}}<ref name=":8" /> He very frequently asked questions and advice of others.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=61–62}} Historian [[James Palais]] argued that Sejong was not a despot; he said that while Sejong was "subjected to criticism and restraint that in other monarchies would be regarded as [[lèse-majesté]]", he was "able to control [his critics] by besting them at their own game rather than by resorting to force and punishment".<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Palais |first=James B. |chapter=Political Leadership in the Yi Dynasty |date=2014-05-01 |title=Political Leadership in Korea |page=7 |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9780295802800-003/html |access-date=2025-07-27 |publisher=[[University of Washington Press]] |language=en |doi=10.1515/9780295802800-003 |isbn=978-0-295-80280-0 |author-link=James Palais}}</ref> Ledyard wrote of Sejong's policymaking, "in everything [Sejong] seems to have had an evenness of judgment, a fairness, common sense, a lack of prejudice".{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=111–112}}

Sejong maintained the policy of ''{{ill|sinmun'go|ko|신문고}}'', wherein commoners with grievances were allowed to beat a drum at the magistrate's office and have their complaint heard.{{sfnm|1a1=Peterson|1y=1992|1p=18|2a1=Kim|2y=2000|2p=5}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=한충희 |script-title=ko:신문고 (申聞鼓) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0032945 |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>

Unlike his predecessors, Sejong regularly and even enthusiastically attended the {{ill|Royal lecture in the Sinosphere|lt=Confucian lectures meant for the king|zh|经筵|ko|경연}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Seth|1y=2010|1p=151|2a1=Oh|2y=2013|2p=63|3a1=Kwŏn|3y=1982|3pp=44–45}} On one occasion, he insisted on attending the lectures even while mourning the death of his father, in order to set an example for future rulers on how important the lectures were.{{Sfn|Volpe|2023|p=259}}<ref name="Annals Lectures">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1422 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:비로소 경연에 나아가다 |trans-chapter=Resumption of attending the royal lectures |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_10411022_005}}</ref> He attended it every day for nearly 22 of his 32 years as king. He assigned around 10 academicians of the Hall of Worthies to research, develop, and deliver the lectures.{{Sfn|Kwŏn|1982|pp=45–46}} He also performed his own research and gave input on the curriculum.{{sfnm|1a1=Kwŏn|1y=1982|1pp=45–46|2a1=Volpe|2y=2023|2pp=265–266}} According to Ledyard's analysis, Sejong's academic interests did not distract from his administrative duties.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=111–112}} Sejong opened the court daily at dawn, and after receiving ceremonial visits, went straight into state meetings.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=9}}

Sejong had a significant impact on curricula for crown princes of Joseon.{{Sfn|Jung|2006|p=134}} In 1421, the crown prince began attending the royal lectures with his father.{{Sfn|Volpe|2023|p=262}} In 1428, he had the {{ill|Chonghak|ko|종학}} established. This institution was directly focused on the education of the royal family, whereas previously, their education was handled by a variety of institutions.{{sfnm|1a1=Jung|1y=2006|1pp=141–142|2a1=Volpe|2y=2023|2p=265}}

Sejong mostly maintained his father's policy of honoring the former royal [[House of Wang]], which had ruled Goryeo. By Sejong's reign, the surviving members of that family were all female. Sejong allowed them to remain aristocrats and live freely. He ordered that the tombs of the former Goryeo monarchs be properly maintained. When several Wang women were involved in legal disputes, Sejong showed amnesty to them. Still, Sejong and his court viewed the women with some suspicion.{{Sfn|Park|2018|pp=40–44}}

Sejong ordered the compilations or revisions of the ''Veritable Records'' of his three predecessors. Under his administration, key practices around the production of the ''Veritable Records'' began, including the practice of making four extra copies of the records for distribution around Korea. This practice would end up saving the ''Veritable Records'' for modern historical use, as most copies were destroyed by the Japanese in 1592, during the Imjin War.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=10}}

=== Legal system ===
Historian Young Kyun Oh argued Sejong attempted to relatively strictly abide by the ''[[Great Ming Code]]'', the Chinese legal code adopted as the basis of Joseon's laws in 1392. Oh evaluated Sejong's deviations from the code as reluctant and minor.{{Sfn|Oh|2013|pp=57–58, 60}} Park evaluated Sejong as resistant to suggestions of punishing people for what he viewed as minor offenses.{{Sfn|Park|2018|p=43}}

Sejong actively participated in revising Joseon's supplementary legal code. In 1420<ref name=":9" /> or 1422,{{Sfn|Park|1992|p=113}} Sejong ordered that the legal code Joseon had been using, the ''{{ill|Kyŏngje yukchŏn|ko|경제육전}}'', be revised. The first draft of the revised code was completed in 1426. Another revision, called the ''[[Sogyukchŏn|Sinsok yukchŏn]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=신속육전|hanja=新續六典|labels=no}}) was completed in 1428. It was revised again and published in 1433 as the ''Sinch'an kyŏngjesok yukchŏn'' ({{Korean|hangul=신찬경제속육전|hanja=新撰經濟續六典|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=이성무 |script-title=ko:대전회통 (大典會通) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0014749 |access-date=2025-07-30 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>).<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=Park |first=Young-Do |date=2006-09-01 |title=King Sejong's Confucian Rule by Law: Focusing on the relationship between law and rule by benevolence |url=https://accesson.kr/rks/v.9/3/103/7574 |journal=The Review of Korean Studies |language=en |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=117–118 |issn=2733-9351 |via=AccessON}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=박병호 |script-title=ko:속육전 (續六典) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0030437 |access-date=2025-07-30 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>{{Sfn|Park|1992|p=113}} A revised version was published in 1435.{{Sfn|Park|1992|p=113}}

Sejong made policies that sought to improve living conditions of prisoners. He ordered that prisoners should be kept in clean prisons, fed regular meals, and not be put in conditions that are excessively cold or hot. He forbade imprisonment of people over 70 or under 15.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2000|1p=5|2a1=Park|2y=1992|2p=116}} He also had [[autopsy]] practices reformed in order to provide more accurate information in legal cases.{{sfnm|1a1=Hong|1a2=Kim|1y=1992|1p=107|2a1=Park|2y=1992|2p=116}}

=== Taxation and economics ===
Sejong significantly reformed the tax system of Joseon. The ''[[taphŏm sonsilpŏp]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=답험손실법|hanja=踏驗損實法|labels=no}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |script-title=ko:답험손실법 (踏驗損實法) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0013861 |access-date=2025-07-29 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>) tax system that had been implemented under his father's reign inadvertantly put excess strain on peasants, especially as tax officials abused the system for their own benefit.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=64–65}} In 1421, Sejong ordered that peasants be allowed to report their own assessments of crop yields, in order to prevent tax officials from making false reports.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=65–66}}<ref name="Annals Tax">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1421 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:호조에서 평안도 관찰사의 관문에 의거하여 올린 손실 사정에 관한 소문 |trans-chapter=Rumors on losses reported by the Ministry of Taxation to the governor of Pyongan Province |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_10309007_007}}</ref>

Work on designing a new tax system, which would eventually be called ''[[kongpŏp]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=공법|hanja=貢法|labels=no}}<ref name=":3">{{Cite encyclopedia |script-title=ko:공법 (貢法) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0004304 |access-date=2025-07-29 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref>), began in 1427.{{Sfn|Park|2005|p=67}} In 1430, Sejong ordered that an extensive public opinion survey on tax policies be conducted across the social classes. Over 170,000 people were polled on; they voted on various issues and proposals, and reasons for voting against Sejong's proposals were thoroughly documented.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=69–70, 86}}<ref name=":3" /> The survey was completed that year. Afterwards, Sejong had his ministers debate the merits of each idea.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=70–73}} The populace voted in favor of Sejong's ideas, but some of his ministers strongly rejected them. The topic was contentious and the debate lasted for 17 years. Sejong was apprehensive of making a sudden change to the tax system, in fear that he could ruin many lives.{{Sfn|Park|2005|pp=76–78, 84–85}} The new system was completed in 1444. It was to be gradually rolled out from localities to larger regions over the following decades.{{Sfn|Park|2005|p=82}} The land tax rate was lowered from 10% of the harvest to 5%.{{sfnm|1a1=Pratt|1y=2007|1p=121|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=204|3a1=Lee|3y=1984|3pp=184–185|4a1=Song et al.|4y=2019|4p=160}} Historians have argued that this tax change improved the quality of life in the country without harming tax income, as confiscations of Buddhist temple land{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=204}} and increases in agricultural productivity helped offset the difference.{{sfn|Song et al.|2019|pp=160–161}} The Hall of Worthies also formulated a variable tax rate that depended on land yields and rainfall conditions.{{sfnm|1a1=Grayson|1y=2002|1p=109|2a1=Lee|2y=1984|2pp=184–185}} 

Sejong continued his father's work in reorganizing the Korean feudal system, in order to improve taxation and the state's ability to mobilize manpower. The organization of the ''[[Hoju|hojŏk]]'' (family registration system) resulted in double the amount of adult males accounted for by the state than during his father's reign.{{Sfn|Duncan|2000|p=136}}
[[File:朝鮮通寳 - Dr. Luke Roberts.jpg|thumb|The [[Joseon Tongbo]] coin, first minted under Sejong]]
Sejong attempted to improve access to and use of [[currency]], to limited success. In 1424, Sejong had the copper coin [[Joseon Tongbo]] minted, but this failed to supplant the predominant practice of bartering cloth and grain.{{Sfn|Wells|2015|p=67}}<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |author=원유한 |script-title=ko:조선통보 (朝鮮通寶) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0052248 |access-date=2025-07-31 |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |language=ko}}</ref> Under Sejong, weights and measures were standardized to promote fairness in trading.{{Sfn|Peterson|Margulies|2010|p=84}}

In 1445, Sejong consolidated the various records of ''sujoji''{{efn|{{Korean|hangul=수조지|hanja=收租地|labels=no}};<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0071206 |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |author=김재명 |lang=ko |script-title=ko:전주 (田主) |trans-title=Chŏnju |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |access-date=2025-08-11}}</ref>}} (land given to government officials in place of salaries), previously managed by various government offices, and placed them under the administration of the [[Six Ministries of Joseon|Ministry of Taxation]] (''Hojo'') to improve transparency in Joseon's fiscal policies.{{sfn|Song et al.|2019|p=162}}

=== Social issues ===
Sejong made multiple attempts to elevate marginalized social groups in Korea, to limited success. In 1423, Sejong attempted to elevate the severely marginalized ''[[ch'ŏnmin]]'' class by dubbing them ''[[paekchŏng]]'' and granting them farmland. Historians have the attempt as unsuccessful; the ''ch'ŏnmin'' continued to be marginalized and work in their hereditary marginalized sectors. The term ''paekchŏng'' began to apply to lower-class people in humble occupations.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=202|2a1=Lee|2y=1984|2p=188}} in 1432, Sejong ordered that the ''paekchŏng'' be allowed to enroll in county schools.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ch'oe |first=Yŏng-Ho |date=1974 |title=Commoners in Early Yi Dynasty Civil Examinations: An Aspect of Korean Social Structure, 1392-1600 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2053128 |journal=The Journal of Asian Studies |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=618 |doi=10.2307/2053128 |jstor=2053128 |issn=0021-9118 |via=[[JSTOR]]}}</ref> Sejong once declared a national amnesty for those imprisoned of minor crimes. He banned slaveholders from arbitrary punishments of slaves.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|p=634}}

In 1426, Sejong enacted a law that granted government serf (''[[nobi]]'') women 100 days of [[Parental leave|maternity leave]] after childbirth. In 1430, this was expanded to include one month before childbirth. In 1434, he also granted the husbands 30 days of paternity leave.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lee |first1=Bae-yong |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p3yW5MdzKnUC&pg=PA267 |title=Women in Korean History |date=20 October 2008 |publisher=Ewha Womans University Press |isbn=978-8973007721 |page=267 |language=en}}</ref> In 1431, Sejong issued a set of laws that set the maximum size of houses for each social class.{{Sfn|Park|2022|p=168}}

Sejong argued that medical treatment should not be limited to the privileged, and that even criminals deserved treatment.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2019|1p=164|2a1=Hong|2a2=Kim|2y=1992|2p=106}}<ref name="Annals Criminals">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1431 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:형조에서 부호할 자가 없는 수인의 구호에 관해 건의하다 |trans-chapter=Proposal on treating sick prisoners |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_11303019_005}}</ref>

Around Sejong's reign, there was a [[Prohibition|prohibition on alcohol consumption]] for non-ceremonial purposes. Even though he was often sick, Sejong refused all medicinal liquors and took only salt water, in order to set a [[Temperance movement|temperate]] example for the populace.{{Sfn|Chung|2014|p=239}}

The issue of whether the state should encourage the playing of the sport [[polo]] was a controversial matter. Bureaucrats saw the sport as emblematic of the excesses of the Goryeo era.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=112}} Spectators would become drunk and rowdy.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Park |first=Eugene Y. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1tg5qc7 |title=Between Dreams and Reality: The Military Examination in Late Chosŏn Korea, 1600–1894 |date=2007 |volume=281 |publisher=[[Harvard University Asia Center]] |isbn=978-0-674-02502-8 |pages=28 |doi=10.2307/j.ctt1tg5qc7 |jstor=j.ctt1tg5qc7 }}</ref> Sejong argued that, while the sport had indeed been played excessively before, it should be kept for military examinations, as he admired the skill and agility required of its players. Ledyard argued Sejong's answer showed judiciousness and nuance.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=112}} In 1425, a polo requirement was officially adopted in military examinations.<ref name=":2" />

=== ''Samganghaengsilto'' ===
[[File:삼강행실도 (1).jpg|thumb|A copy of the ''{{ill|Samganghaengsilto|ko|삼강행실도}}'']]
In 1428, a legal case was brought to Sejong's attention. A man named [[Kim Hwa]] ({{Korean|hangul=김화|hanja=金禾|labels=no}}) [[Patricide|murdered his father]]. This was seen as an egregious offense against a fundamental Confucian relationship.{{sfnm|1a1=Oh|1y=2013|1pp=56–63|2a1=Yoo|2y=2006|2p=18}} Minister {{ill|Hŏ Cho|ko|허조}} proposed that Sejong apply the older and more draconian ''[[Tang Code]]'', in order to exact a harsher punishment on Kim. Sejong refused this proposal, although the matter concerned him deeply. He brought the matter to the Hall of Worthies and explored how Confucian values could be better reinforced in the populace.{{Sfn|Oh|2013|pp=56–63}}

It was decided that a book providing examples of Confucian ethics could help educate the public. This resulted in the creation of the 1434 book ''{{ill|Samganghaengsilto|ko|삼강행실도}}''.{{Sfn|Oh|2013|pp=62, 64–67}} The text was meant to improve the lives and morals of the general populace. It compiled Chinese and Korean stories and anecdotes that illustrated ethical Confucian behavior. It also included large pictures for the sake of the illiterate.{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1p=236|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2pp=128–131|3a1=Kim|3y=2012|3pp=213–214}} The text was initially published in Hanja and later translated into Hangul. The Hangul translation efforts later sparked backlash from Hall of Worthies scholars, including {{ill|Chŏng Ch'angson|ko|정창손}} and [[Ch'oe Malli]].{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1p=236|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1997|2pp=34–35}} Its Hangul translation was completed in 1481, decades after Sejong's death.{{Sfn|Lee|Ramsey|2011|pp=108–109}}

=== Buddhism ===
While Sejong and his predecessors privately practiced Buddhism, their policies restricted the power and influence of Buddhist institutions.{{sfnm|1a1=Duncan|1y=2000|1pp=251–252|2a1=Ahn|2y=2025|2pp=197–202|3a1=Kim|3y=1992|3p=27|4a1=Lovins|4y=2019|4p=279}}

Joseon's predecessor Goryeo had been deeply Buddhist. But around the Goryeo–Joseon transition in the late 14th-century, anti-Buddhist sentiment had grown to new heights among Confucianists.{{Sfn|Duncan|2000|pp=251–252}} Confucianists criticized the financial impact of the religion on the state (Buddhist temples were significant land and slaveholders and monks were seen as unproductive{{Sfn|Pu|2005|pp=34–35}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kim |first=Sung-Eun Thomas |date=2016 |title=Perception of Monastic Slaves by Scholar-Officials and Monks in the Late Koryŏ and Early Chosŏn Periods |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24892365 |journal=Journal of Korean Religions |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=12–14, 28 |jstor=24892365 |issn=2093-7288 |via=[[JSTOR]]}}</ref>{{sfnm|1a1=Ahn|1y=2025|1pp=200–202|2a1=Seth|2y=2010|2p=156|3a1=Kim|3y=2007|3p=141}}), as well as its philosophical foundations. Many of these Confucianists became significant members of the new Joseon bureaucracy.{{Sfn|Duncan|2000|pp=251–252}} Many in Sejong's court were actively hostile to Buddhism.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=116–117|2a1=Pu|2y=2005|2pp=37–38}} {{ill|Yun Hoe|ko|윤회 (조선)}}, deputy director of the Hall of Worthies, wrote in 1424 to Sejong that "[w]e consider the harm of Buddhists to be prevalent still. Since the Han period the reverence for Buddha has been increasingly fervent, yet neither happiness nor profit has been gained... We think of all the heterodox teachings, Buddhism is the worst".{{Sfn|Seth|2010|p=156}}<ref name="Annals Worst">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1424 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:불교의 개혁·《가례》에 따른 상제의 시행과 관련한 집현전 제학 윤회 등의 상소문 |trans-chapter=A petition from Yun Hoe of the Hall of Worthies on the reform of Buddhism and implementation of sangje in accordance with the Book of Rites |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_10603008_002}}</ref> On the other hand, a significant majority of people outside the government actively practiced Buddhism.{{Sfn|Kim|2007|pp=142–143}}

Unlike the Confucianists, Sejong believed that Buddhism and Confucianism could coexist, although he was critical of the economic impact that the religion was having on Joseon.{{Sfn|Pu|2005|pp=31–32, 42–43}} Sejong's policies significantly restricted the influence of Buddhism on Joseon.{{sfnm|1a1=Pu|1y=2005|1pp=36–37|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2pp=116–117|3a1=Pratt|3y=2007|3pp=124–125}}<ref name="Buswell Jr.">{{Cite book |last=Buswell Jr. |first=Robert E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FqjxsF6mblMC |title=Culture and the State in Late Chosŏn Korea |date=1999 |publisher=Harvard Univ Asia Center Familial deaths in the mid-1440s deepened Sejong's devotion to Buddhism.
