Grief-stricken, He has come to let belief in [[karma]] fill the void in his heart".{{efn|{{lang|ko|임금이 두 대군(大君)을 연달아 잃고, 왕후가 이어 승하하니, 슬퍼함이 지극하여 인과화복(因果禍福)의 말이 드디어 그 마음의 허전한 틈에 들어맞았다}}; {{lang|ko|上連喪二大君, 王后繼薨, 悲哀憾愴, 因果禍福之說, 遂中其隙}}}}{{sfn|Kim|2007|p=148}}<ref name="Annals Grief">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1449 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:박강·조완벽·김수온에게 관직을 제수하다 |trans-chapter=Pak Kang, Cho Wanbyŏk, and Kim Suon are granted official posts |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_13102025_002}}</ref> Sejong had temples hold memorial ceremonies for Sohŏn.{{Sfn|Pu|2005|p=28}} By 1445, he was practicing [[Buddhist vegetarianism]].{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=124}} In 1448 and 1449, Sejong had a Buddhist shrine built on the palace grounds.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=116–117|2a1=Duncan|2y=2000|2p=255}} In 1449, when Sejong fell ill, he invited the monk [[Sinmi]] to conduct Buddhist services in the palace. The following year, Sinmi was granted honorary titles of respect.{{Sfn|Duncan|2000|p=253}} Grayson wrote that Sejong "died in the bosom of Buddhism".{{Sfn|Grayson|2002|p=109}}

=== Other religions ===
Sejong, like most other Joseon kings, disapproved of [[Korean shamanism]]. Beginning with the reign of Sejong, [[Mu (shaman)|Korean shamans]] were barred from entering the capital. However, he appointed some shamans to posts in the public health organization outside the capital {{ill|Hwarinsŏ|ko|활인서}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baker |first=Don |date=2014 |title=Seoul and Salem: Contrasts in How States Treated Female Performers of Licentious Rituals |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24329483 |journal=Journal of Korean Religions |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=22 |jstor=24329483 |issn=2093-7288}}</ref>

In 1427, Sejong issued a decree against the Huihui ([[Islam in Korea|Korean Muslim]]) community that had enjoyed special status and [[Stipend|stipends]] since the [[Yuan dynasty]]'s [[Goryeo under Mongol rule|rule over Goryeo]]. The Huihui were forced to abandon their headgear, close down their ceremonial hall—a [[mosque]] in Gaegyeong, present-day [[Kaesong]]—and worship like everyone else.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Baker |first=Don |date=6 December 2006 |title=Islam Struggles for a Toehold in Korea |url=http://www.asiaquarterly.com/content/view/167/43/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516063253/http://www.asiaquarterly.com/content/view/167/43/ |archive-date=16 May 2008 |access-date=28 September 2023 |journal=Harvard Asia Quarterly |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=25–30}}</ref>{{Sfn|Wang|2023|p=75}}

== Foreign policy ==
Sejong continued the [[Tang dynasty|Tang]] and Goryeo tradition of ''[[Xianghua (policy)|xianghua]]'' ({{Korean/auto|hangul=향화|hanja=向化|mr=yes|labels=no|order=zhm}};<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |script-title=ko:향화 왜인 |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Local Culture]] |url=https://busan.grandculture.net/Contents?local=busan&dataType=01&contents_id=GC04203994 |access-date=2025-07-28 |author=한문종 |language=ko |trans-title=Hyanghwa Japanese}}</ref> "submitting-foreigner status"{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|pp=41–42}}). This was a semi-hereditary set of designations for foreigners that allowed them to reside in Korea, with certain tax and civil exemptions for at least one generation; their descendents were eventually naturalized. The status's intent was to encourage peaceful, eventual naturalization and assimilation.{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|pp=41–44}} For settlers around the capital, Sejong had the designation limited to one generation after the original immigrants.{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|p=43}}<ref name="Annals Xianghua">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1439 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:의정부에서 향화인의 시재에 대해 아뢰다 |trans-chapter=State Council report on xianghua peoples |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12105029_001}}</ref> Joseon, under Sejong, also had separate pathways for naturalization of foreigners, including the granting of [[Korean clans|clan seats]].{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|pp=43–44}}

Sejong also continued the practice of allowing systematized forms of [[tribute]] from foreigners, namely Jurchens and Japanese people. Depending on group and status, a limited number of tributes were allowed to be given to the monarchy in exchange for political favor.{{Sfn|Robinson|2013|pp=356–357}}

=== Japan–Korea relations ===
{{See also|History of Japan–Korea relations}}
[[File:PB9C-15C 001 三綱行實圖 삼강행실도 109 (cropped).jpg|thumb|316x316px|''Wokou'' (center), depiction from ''{{ill|Samganghaengsilto|ko|삼강행실도}}'', produced during Sejong's reign]]
Sejong and his administration caused a decrease in raids from Japanese pirates (called ''[[wokou]]'') and increase in trade with Japan.{{Sfn|Lee|2006|pp=157–159}} Due to the peaceful contact and trade, historian James B. Lewis described the 15th century encompassing Sejong's reign as "the peak of peaceful Japanese contact with Korea prior to the end of the twentieth century".{{Sfn|Lewis|2003|p=20}}

Although pirates from [[Tsushima Island]] raided Joseon's shores with declining frequency by the late Goryeo period, they still posed a threat by Sejong's reign.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|pp=209–201}} The pirates would steal materials, boats, and Korean people for enslavement.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=101}} In 1418, a famine and the death of Tsushima leader {{ill|Sō Sadashige|ja|宗貞茂|ko}} led to increased raids on Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=105}} In retaliation for this, in 1419, Sejong, under his father's guidance,<ref name=":7" />{{Sfn|Lee|2006|pp=161–162}} launched the punitive [[Ōei Invasion]] against Tsushima.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1pp=209–201|2a1=Robinson|2y=1992|2pp=105–106}} Joseon forces consisted of 227 ships and some 17,000 soldiers under command of [[Yi Chongmu]].{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1pp=209–201|2a1=Lee|2y=2006|2pp=162–163}} After 15 days of fighting, the lord of Tsushima surrendered.{{Sfn|Kim|2012|pp=209–201}} During this conflict, Japanese people that fled Tsushima were allowed to settle in Joseon as ''hyanghwa''.{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|p=44}}

Joseon attempted to incorporate Tsushima into its own territory.{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=2006|1pp=165–166|2a1=Robinson|2y=1996|2p=32}} Ten days before Joseon's punitive attack on Tsushima, Taejong claimed that Tsushima once belonged to Korea. Seven months afterwards, in 1420, the Korean court accepted a request of Tsushima lord [[Sō Sadamori]] (or someone claiming to represent Sadamori) that Tsushima be absorbed into Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1996|p=32}} The Joseon court then considered Tsushima to be under the administrative boundaries of [[Gyeongsang Province]].{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=106}} This absorption was later rejected by Sadamori.{{Sfn|Robinson|1996|p=32}} Ultimately, the absorption failed to occur.{{Sfn|Lee|2006|p=166}}

Under Sejong, Joseon successfully incentivized Japanese leaders to discourage piracy in exchange for valuable trade access. Through this strategy, Joseon was able to change its focus from security to trade management.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|pp=105–107, 110}} From Taejong's reign to Sejong's, raids dropped from 4.3 invasions per year to 1.8 and trade missions increased from 20.4 per year to 31.3.{{Sfn|Lee|2006|pp=157–159}} Japanese traders were restricted to all but {{ill|three ports of Joseon|ko|삼포 개항}}; the third port was opened under Sejong in 1426.{{Efn|Ports were located at Pusanp'o (now part of [[Busan]]), Naeip'o (now part of [[Changwon]]), and Yŏmp'o (now part of [[Ulsan]]).{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1pp=209–210|2a1=Pratt|2y=2007|2p=131|3a1=Lewis|3y=2003|3p=18}}}}{{sfnm|1a1=Lewis|1y=2003|1pp=20–21|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2pp=209–201|3a1=Robinson|3y=1992|3p=104}} Japanese traders were also made to follow specific routes on specific days to reach the capital.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=106}} In 1423, government warehouses were created for Japanese traders in the ports.{{Sfn|Lewis|2003|pp=20–21}} In 1438, Joseon granted Tsushima lord [[Sō Sadamori]] a monopoly on issuing documents of passage for Japanese people to visit Joseon.{{sfnm|1a1=Lewis|1y=2003|1p=20|2a1=Robinson|2y=1992|2pp=106–107}} This also benefitted Joseon in that it allowed them to offshore this administrative process and the possible associated backlash from rebuffed Japanese traders.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=111}} In 1439, some limited exceptions to the monopoly were granted to other Japanese lords.{{sfnm|1a1=Lewis|1y=2003|1p=20|2a1=Robinson|2y=1992|2pp=106–107}} In the 1443 [[Treaty of Kyehae]], Joseon limited the number of ships at these ports from Japan to 50 per year.{{sfnm|1a1=Robinson|1y=1992|1p=107|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2pp=209–201|3a1=Lewis|3y=2003|3p=20|4a1=Lee|4y=1984|4pp=191–192}}

Scholars have debated how Joseon under Sejong treated Japan. Several have argued that Joseon treated parts of Japan as if they were subordinate to Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1996|pp=23–25}} Envoys from even the [[shogun]] were symbolically ceremonially treated as if the shogun was a subject of Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|pp=101–103}} Japanese leaders were made to request copper seals ({{Korean/auto|hangul=도서|hanja=圖書|hanjaref=<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |url=https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0015696 |script-title=ko:도서 (圖書) |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]] |publisher=[[Academy of Korean Studies]] |lang=ko |trans-title=Tosŏ |access-date=2025-07-28 |author=이근호}}</ref>|mr=yes|labels=no}}) in order to access Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|pp=105–106}} Japanese leaders that showed greater aptitude in preventing piracy were granted greater rank and trade with Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|pp=105–107}} Historian Kenneth R. Robinson argued that Joseon had a unique and flexible relationship with the fractured "Japan" (Japan was not a strongly unified political entity by this time) that changed over time. He argued Joseon borrowed elements of China's tributary system for its own purposes.{{Sfn|Robinson|1996|pp=40–42}}

Japanese leaders frequently requested Buddhist gifts from Joseon.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2017|1p=109|2a1=Pu|2y=2005|2pp=40–41}} For example, the [[Ōuchi clan]] persistently requested the wood printing blocks of the ''[[Tripitaka Koreana]]'', to the chagrin of Sejong's Confucianist court. The blocks were valuable and expensive to produce copies of. Eventually, the Ōuchi clan was given printed copies of the ''Tripitaka'' instead, which were still expensive to produce.{{Sfn|Kim|2017|p=109}}

=== Northern frontier and Jurchen relations ===
Sejong continued the work of his predecessors in pacifying and conquering the northern frontier. It was under Sejong that Korea's northern borders were expanded to reach their approximate current extent.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1pp=208–209|2a1=Seth|2y=2010|2pp=144–145}} The northern frontier was of strategic importance, as it served as the border between Korea and China, and because the local [[Jurchen people|Jurchens]] would frequently raid Korean settlements.{{sfnm|1a1=Jackson|1y=2025|1pp=104–105|2a1=Seth|2y=2010|2pp=144–145|3a1=Robinson|3y=1992|3pp=97–98}} In 1432, the Hulun Udeha tribe (Eastern Jurchens) attacked Joseon.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=100}}

Sejong launched military campaigns against the Jurchens and established garrison forces to pacify local populations.{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1p=230|2a1=Jackson|2y=2025|2pp=104–105}} He sent one such campaign in 1433, with {{ill|Ch'oe Yundŏk|ko|최윤덕}} and {{ill|Yi Ch'ŏn|ko|이천 (1376년)}} in command, and another in 1437 under [[Kim Chongsŏ]].{{Sfn|Kim|2012|pp=208–209}} The latter campaign resulted in the creation of {{ill|Yukchin|lt=six garrisons in the region|ko|육진}} and the current northern borders of Korea.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1pp=208–209|2a1=Seth|2y=2010|2pp=144–145}}

Sejong also opened trade with Jurchens in order to discourage raids. This was possibly, in part, motivated by their previous successes in using trade to discourage Japanese piracy.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|p=110}} From 1437 to 1443, the Hulun Udeha tribe that had previously attacked Joseon sent at least 127 trade missions to the Joseon court. Over time, restrictions and limits were applied on Jurchen trade missions to Joseon. Such trade was intended to provide Jurchens economic alternatives to raiding.{{Sfn|Robinson|1992|pp=100–101}} Jurchens that aided Joseon were rewarded with rank and access to trade. His administration also moved Korean settlers to conquered regions and encouraged intermarriage between Jurchens and Koreans to deter conflict.{{sfnm|1a1=Jackson|1y=2025|1pp=104–105|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2pp=144–145|3a1=Kim|3y=2012|3pp=208–209|4a1=Bohnet|4y=2020|4p=47|5a1=Robinson|5y=1992|5pp=98–99}} During Sejong's reign, the entire population of [[Hamgyong Province]] north of [[Tanchon]] was described as the descendants of Jurchen ''hyanghwa''. They eventually became full citizens of Joseon.{{Sfn|Bohnet|2020|p=45}} Jurchens were also granted nominal appointments to the Korean military. These appointments did not require military service; they were instead meant to assimilate by integrating Jurchens into the Joseon bureaucracy.{{Sfn|Robinson|2013|p=347}}

Historians have evaluated Sejong's efforts in settling and pacifying the region as having mixed success.{{sfnm|1a1=Jackson|1y=2025|1pp=104–105|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2pp=144–145|3a1=Kim|3y=2012|3pp=208–209}} Korean settlers struggled to make a living in the frontier and often abandoned the land.{{Sfn|Jackson|2025|pp=104–105}} The northern regions would continue to pose threats to Joseon's security after Sejong's reign.{{sfnm|1a1=Jackson|1y=2025|1pp=104–105|2a1=Park|2y=2022|2pp=144–145|3a1=Kim|3y=2012|3pp=208–209}}

=== China–Korea relations ===
{{See also|History of Sino-Korean relations|Tributary system of China}}

Historian Shih-Shan Henry Tsai argued that the reign of Sejong saw an improvement in Sino-Korean relations and that "Sino-Korean borders became marketplaces instead of war zones". Sejong and the Ming [[Yongle Emperor]] often exchanged books and letters on various topics, including religion, philosophy, history, science, and technology. In 1423 alone, Sejong sent 10,000 tribute horses to Yongle. In return, Sejong received a huge quantity of silver, [[brocade]], and [[silk]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tsai |first=Shih-Shan Henry |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvcwncr9 |title=Perpetual Happiness: The Ming Emperor Yongle |date=2001 |publisher=[[University of Washington Press]] |isbn=978-0-295-98109-3 |pages=192–193 |jstor=j.ctvcwncr9 }}</ref> Sejong had the gate [[Yŏngŭnmun]] erected in Seoul in 1429 as a symbolic place of greeting for arriving Chinese envoys.{{Sfn|Pratt|2007|p=186}}

Sejong sought to balance the Joseon policy of ''[[sadae]]'' (Confucian deference to China) with the need for flexible governance and Korean autonomy.{{sfnm|1a1=Yoo|1y=2006|1pp=14–16|2a1=Robinson|2y=1996|2pp=40–42}} For example, a number of historians have argued that the semi-tributary relationships Sejong maintained with Japanese and Jurchen groups were technically forbidden by the Chinese tributary system. Under that system, tributaries to China could only interact with each other as equals, but Sejong chose to forego strict adherence to this for Joseon's benefit.{{Sfn|Robinson|1996|pp=23–24}} Also, in at least one occasion early in his reign, Sejong expressed reluctance to perform ritual sacrifices to pray for rain; such rituals were seen as only appropriate for the Chinese emperor. Despite this, he eventually began performing the rituals.{{Sfn|Kang|2006b|pp=82–83}} By the end of his reign, he stopped this practice.{{Sfn|Deuchler|2015|pp=62–63}} Sejong had a scholar write an essay that said that Korean kings also had the [[Mandate of Heaven]], which was normally exclusively claimed by China.{{Sfn|Nahm|1996|p=116}} In 1449, when Ming requested that Joseon send 100,000 Korean troops to the [[Liaodong Peninsula|Liaodong]] area of [[Manchuria]], Joseon declined.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=Ji-Young |date=2013 |title=Diplomatic Ritual as a Power Resource: The Politics of Asymmetry in Early Modern Chinese-Korean Relations |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23418779 |journal=Journal of East Asian Studies |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=323 |doi=10.1017/S1598240800003957 |jstor=23418779 |issn=1598-2408 |via=[[JSTOR]]}}</ref>

The anti-Buddhist policies under Sejong put Joseon at odds with Ming; in dealings with China, the Joseon court attempted to allay concerns that it was suppressing Buddhism. Around that time, Buddhism enjoyed significant support among the Ming court and gentry. Korean Buddhist monks escaped to Ming: 30 during the reign of Taejong and 9 during the reign of Sejong.{{Sfn|Kim|2017|pp=105–107}} Sejong asked the Yongle Emperor, a devout Buddhist, if those monks could be repatriated. Fearing what would happen to the monks, the Yongle Emperor declined.{{sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2017|1pp=105–107|2a1=Pu|2y=2005|2p=41}}

== Hangul ==
{{Main|Origin of Hangul|Hangul}}

Sejong was responsible for the development of Hangul, the native alphabet for the Korean language. It is debated to what extent Sejong was personally involved in its creation, although most scholars believe he was significantly involved.{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=2009|1p=14|2a1=Ahn|2y=2004|2p=6}} A minority of scholars believe that Sejong was the sole author. All contemporary documentary evidence suggests that he was,{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=1997|1pp=14–19|2a1=Haarmann|2y=1993|2pp=151–152}}<ref name=":42">{{Cite book |last=Gnanadesikan |first=Amalia E. |url=https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Writing+Revolution%3A+Cuneiform+to+the+Internet-p-9781405154079 |title=The Writing Revolution: Cuneiform to the Internet |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-444-35985-5 |pages=196–197, 203}}</ref>{{Sfn|Ahn|2004|p=6}} but many scholars argue Sejong would have been too busy to develop Hangul on his own.{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=1997|1pp=14–19|2a1=Lee|2y=2009|2p=13}}

Before the invention of Hangul, Korea had been using [[Hanja]] ([[Chinese characters]]), as well as related systems like [[Idu script|Idu]] and [[Hyangchal]], since antiquity. The difficulty of the systems limited their use to mostly upper-class people; commoners were largely illiterate.{{sfnm|1a1=Sohn|1y=2001|1p=122|2a1=Oh|2y=2013|2pp=140–141|3a1=Haarmann|3y=1993|3pp=144–145}} Also, the scripts are not well suited for representing the [[Korean language]]; the Chinese and Korean [[Language family|languages are not closely related]] and differ in significant ways.{{sfnm|1a1=Wang|1y=2023|1pp=70–71|2a1=Haarmann|2y=1993|2p=145|3a1=Kim-Renaud|3y=2000|3p=18}} Korean pronunciation and ideas could only be indirectly represented.{{Sfnm|1a1=Lee|1a2=Ramsey|1y=2011|1pp=1–2|2a1=Kim|2y=2005|2pp=3, 7–9|3a1=Oh|3y=2013|3pp=140–142}}

Due to a lack of records on the topic, it is not known when work on Hangul first began. A number of scholars have argued that the creation of the 1434 ''Samganghaengsilto'' caused Sejong to become interested in universal literacy.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=130–131|2a1=Lee|2y=2009|2pp=15–16|3a1=Yoo|3y=2006|3pp=31–32}} Also, Sejong long had a personal interest in linguistics and languages. He took a personal interest in the activities of the [[Bureau of Interpreters]], and himself took Chinese lessons from early on in his reign.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=109–111, 120|2a1=Wang|2y=2014|2pp=60, 71|3a1=Volpe|3y=2025|3p=57}} A 1435 record claimed that Sejong practiced colloquial spoken Chinese every other day and took lessons from famed linguist {{ill|Yi Pyŏn|ko|이변 (1391년)}}.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=109–110}} Hangul was possibly developed in secret, in anticipation of the backlash that it eventually received, although this is debated.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1990|1p=15|2a1=Ahn|2y=2004|2pp=12–14, 16–22}} 

The script was revealed, likely mostly completed, to Sejong's court in the 12th month of 1443.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=85, 134–136|2a1=Yoo|2y=2006|2p=32}} In the 2nd month of 1444, a major faction in the Hall of Worthies led by [[Ch'oe Malli]] made a famous rebuke of the script. Ch'oe and several others argued that Hangul was anti-Confucian, as they felt it was too far a departure from Chinese civilization.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=150–151|2a1=Nahm|2y=1996|2p=120|3a1=Wang|3y=2014|3p=60|4a1=Yoo|4y=2006|4p=26}} Sejong rebutted that he felt the script was Confucian, as it was created out of a desire to benefit his subjects.{{Sfn|Yoo|2006|p=26}} Anti-Hangul sentiment was also partially motivated by elitism; literacy in Hanja was then seen as a status symbol, and promoting general literacy could be seen as harming the social positions of the elite.{{Sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=150–152|2a1=Kim|2y=2012|2p=211|3a1=Haarmann|3y=1993|3pp=152–154|4a1=Song|4y=2006|4pp=47–48}} The script was initially dubbed ''ŏnmun'' ({{Korean|hangul=언문|hanja=諺文|labels=no|lit=vernacular script}}), which developed an elitist connotation of "vulgar writing".{{sfnm|1a1=Kim-Renaud|1y=2000|1pp=17–18|2a1=Pratt|2y=2007|2p=122|3a1=Ramsey|3y=1992|3p=44|4a1=Song|4y=2006|4pp=47–48}} Sejong had Ch'oe and several others imprisoned for a single day.{{sfnm|1a1=Yoo|1y=2006|1p=29|2a1=Kang|2y=2006a|2p=236|3a1=Ledyard|3y=1998|3p=149}} 

At some point,{{Efn|The office's official establishment is recorded in the ''Veritable Records'' as on the 8th day, 11th month of 1446,<ref name="Annals Onmunchong">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1446 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:《태조실록》을 어효첨과 양성지로 하여금 초록하여 바치게 하였다 |trans-chapter=Ŏ Hyoch'ŏm and Yang Sŏngji are made to transcribe and present the Veritable Records of Taejo |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12811008_001}}</ref> but Ledyard argues the office was likely active before this, likely soon after Sejong announced the script. Either way, scholarly work was actively being performed on Hangul before 1446.{{sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=139–140}}}} Sejong recruited young men of the Hall of Worthies for a new office dedicated to Hangul that was dubbed {{ill|Ŏnmunch'ŏng|ko|언문청}} ({{lit|Vernacular Script Commission}}).{{Efn|Ledyard argues that ''Ŏnmunch'ŏng'' was likely not the name of the department at the time, and that that name was likely inserted into the ''Veritable Records of Sejong'' by anti-Hangul literati.{{sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=156}} The office's official establishment is recorded in the ''Veritable Records'' as on the 8th day, 11th month of 1446,<ref name="Annals Onmunchong">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1446 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:《태조실록》을 어효첨과 양성지로 하여금 초록하여 바치게 하였다 |trans-chapter=Ŏ Hyoch'ŏm and Yang Sŏngji are made to transcribe and present the Veritable Records of Taejo |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12811008_001}}</ref> but Ledyard argues the office was likely active before this, likely soon after Sejong announced the script. Either way, scholarly work was actively being performed on Hangul before 1446.{{sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=139–140}}}}{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=139–140|2a1=Paek|2y=2011|2p=3|3a1=Lee|3y=1984|3pp=191–192}} It worked on developing official documentation for Hangul. It also worked on several major literary projects related to Hangul, including the 1447 rhyme dictionary ''[[Tongguk chŏngun]]'' and the first major piece of Hangul literature ''[[Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga]]''.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1pp=327–329, 370|2a1=Volpe|2y=2025|2pp=63–64|3a1=Kim|3y=2007|3p=147}}
[[File:Hunminjeongum.jpg|thumb|First page of the ''[[Hunminjeongeum|Hunminjeongeum Haerye]]'', showing the intro by Sejong]] 

In the 9th month of 1446, Hangul's documentation was completed and published in the texts ''[[Hunminjeongeum]]'' and its companion commentary text ''[[Hunminjeongeum Haerye]]''. The ''Hunminjeongeum'' was penned by Sejong himself, while the ''Haerye'' was compiled by a group of scholars of the Ŏnmunch'ŏng led by [[Chŏng Inji]].{{sfnm|1a1=Kang|1y=2006a|1p=231|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2pp=161–162|3a1=Ramsey|3y=1992|3pp=44–45}} The ''Hunminjeongeum'' begins with this now-famous quote:{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=170|2a1=Wang|2y=2014|2p=60|3a1=Kim-Renaud|3y=2000|3p=17}}{{Blockquote|text=The sounds of our country's language are different from those of the [[Names of China|Middle Kingdom]] and are not confluent with the sounds of characters. Therefore, among the ignorant people, there have been many who, having something they want to put into words, have in the end been unable to express their feelings. I have been distressed because of this, and have newly designed twenty-eight letters, which I wish to have everyone practice at their ease and make convenient for their daily use.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=170|2a1=Kim|2y=2000|2p=7|3a1=Kim-Renaud|3y=2000|3p=17}}|author=Sejong the Great|source=preface|title=''Hunminjeongeum''}}Sejong attempted to lightly pressure his detractors and subjects into accepting the script, to limited success.{{sfnm|1a1=Ledyard|1y=1998|1p=379|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1997|2p=73|3a1=Yoo|3y=2006|3p=33}} Ledyard argues that Sejong intentionally did not aggressively force the script on others as to avoid more severe backlash. Ledyard evaluated this hypothesized strategy favorably and said it likely contributed to Hangul's eventual success.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1997|p=73}} He attempted to integrate Hangul into bureaucratic examinations and the curricula of government schools like the [[Sŏnggyun'gwan]], although such integrations were often removed after his death.{{Sfn|Paek|2011|p=6}}<ref name="Annals exam">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1446 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:이과와 이전의 취재에 훈민정음을 시험하게 하였다 |trans-chapter=The igwa and ichŏn are made to include exams on the Hunminjŏngŭm |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12812026_003}}</ref>

Despite Sejong's efforts, Hangul continued to be looked down upon until the end of the Joseon period, over 400 years later.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=152}} It was only officially adopted by the government in 1894, during the [[Kabo Reform]].{{Sfn|Paek|2011|pp=21–22}}

== Later life and death ==
Sejong reported to having recurring and worsening health issues for much of his life; a number of these complaints were recorded in the ''Veritable Records''.{{sfn|Lee|2021|pp=203, 205}}<ref name="Annals Back">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1435 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:진양 대군 이유에게 대신 전별연을 행하게 하다 |trans-chapter=Grand Prince Chinyang to host farewell party instead |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_11704001_001}}</ref><ref name="Annals Disease">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1438 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:이징옥 김효성을 대신하여 경원을 지킬 장수와 세자섭정을 문의하다 |trans-chapter=Yi Chingok asks on Kim Hyosŏng's behalf for a general to guard Kyongwon and inquiry about the regency of the crown prince |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12004028_004}}</ref> One of the earliest records of his complaints was made when he was 22 years old; he then claimed to have knee and back pain. In his 30s, he complained of back pain and began reporting problems with his vision, [[Polydipsia|excess thirst]], and [[Frequent urination|excess urination]]. In his 40s, he complained of his vision problems with greater frequency.{{sfn|Lee|2021|p=205}} He had a reputation for enjoying the consumption of meat and having a sedentary lifestyle.{{sfn|Lee|2021|pp=203, 205}} Beginning in 1445, he was practicing [[Buddhist vegetarianism]].{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|p=124}}

Scholars have attempted to [[Retrospective diagnosis|infer what diseases he had based on historical evidence]]. The predominant hypotheses are that Sejong had either [[Type 1 diabetes|type 1]] or [[type 2 diabetes]].{{Efn|Sources that express support for the diabetes hypothesis:{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=1997|1p=28|2a1=Ledyard|2y=1998|2p=124}}}}{{sfn|Lee|2021|p=205}} Medical researcher JiHwan Lee disputes that diagnosis and argues that Sejong's symptoms more closely resemble those of [[ankylosing spondylitis]] (a type of arthritis). Lee argues that either type of diabetes would have been lethal to him sooner, and that Sejong did not have a clear family history of diabetes.{{sfn|Lee|2021|p=205}}

Beginning in 1437, Sejong began asking his ministers if lesser governmental affairs could be delegated to the crown prince, as he was feeling unwell.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=113–116}} Historian [[Martina Deuchler]] argued Sejong asked this because he intended to ease the crown prince into politics to make the succession smoother.{{Sfn|Deuchler|2015|p=61}} His ministers dismissed his health concerns then and multiple times over for years onwards, including in 1438, 1439, and 1442.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=113–116}} In 1439, he stopped attending the royal lectures due to his health issues.{{Sfn|Kim|2007|p=151}} Finally, apparently frustrated with the lack of progress, Sejong issued an edict in 1443 in which he declared the crown prince would handle minor state affairs for the last half of each month, and that all ministers must proclaim their loyalty to him. This sparked furious protest from across the government. Some ministers balked at the idea of being presided over by the crown prince, and others expressed concerns that the division of royal authority could destabilize the state. After years of debate and compromise, in 1445, the crown prince began to handle the routine affairs of government.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=113–116}} Historian Kim Jongmyung argues that Sejong then devoted himself wholeheartedly to working on Hangul.{{Sfn|Kim|2007|p=150}}
[[File:여주 영릉과 영릉 세종 영릉 능침(항공).jpg|thumb|[[Yeongneung]]: the tomb of Sejong]]
In his last years, Sejong spent much of his time in his study, writing poetry.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1998|pp=116–117}} Even while in deep pain, Sejong reportedly insisted on learning and attending lectures, and would even stay up past midnight to do so.{{Sfn|Ahn|2004|p=15}} In 1446, after the promulgation of Hangul, he said to his ministers that he was "suffering from various illnesses and just waiting in the palace for death".{{sfn|Kim|2017|p=145}}<ref name="Annals Dying">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |year=1446 |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:집현전에서 왕비를 위한 불경 편찬의 뜻을 거둘 것을 아뢰나 받아 들이지 아니하다 |trans-chapter=Rejected request from the Hall of Worthies to cancel the compilation of Buddhist scriptures in honor of the Queen |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_12803028_002}}</ref> In the last months of his life, his pains grew more serious.{{Sfn|Ledyard|1990|p=18}} On the 22nd day, 1st month of 1450, he moved into the residence of [[Grand Prince Hyoryŏng]] to receive treatment for his illnesses.{{Sfn|Kim|2019|p=158}}<ref name="Annals Residence">{{cite book |author=Office of Annals |title=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |title-link=Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty |publisher=[[National Institute of Korean History]] |language=Korean |script-chapter=ko:총효령 대군 집으로 이어하다 |date=1450 |trans-chapter=Moved to Grand prince Hyoryŏng's residence |chapter-url=https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kda_13201022_001}}</ref> He died on the 17th day, 2nd month of 1450 at the age of 52, in the residence of {{ill|Grand Prince Yŏngŭng|ko|영응대군}} in Gyeongbokgung's East Palace.{{Sfn|Kim|2000|p=4}}<ref name="Annals Death" /> He was the first Joseon king to die while in office.{{Sfn|Deuchler|2015|p=61}} He is buried in the tomb [[Yeongneung]]. That tomb was originally located in what is now [[Seocho District]] in Seoul, but in 1469 it was moved to what is now [[Yeoju]] after it was determined that the geomantic properties of the new site were superior. He is buried alongside [[Queen Sohŏn]].{{Sfn|Korea Foundation|2011|pp=84–85}}

== Reception and legacy ==
[[File:10000_won_serieVI_obverse.jpeg|thumb|right|King Sejong the Great, as depicted on the [[Bank of Korea]]'s 10,000 [[South Korean won|won]] banknote (Series VI).]]
Sejong has been evaluated by a number of historians as the greatest monarch in Korean history.{{Sfnm|1a1=Kim|1y=2012|1p=189|2a1=Korea Foundation|2y=2011|2p=113|3a1=Seth|3y=2010|3pp=150–151|4a1=Wells|4y=2015|4p=91}} His reign has been described as a [[Golden Age]] by various historians.{{Sfnm|1a1=Park|1y=2018|1p=40|2a1=Park|2y=1992|2p=113|3a1=Jeon|3y=2011|3p=395|4a1=Kim|4y=2019|4p=136}}<ref name=":10" /> Of all kings of Joseon, his name is mentioned the most throughout the ''Veritable Records'': over 2000 times.{{Sfn|Kim|2007|p=136}} Sejong has since served as a legendary figure in Korean science. His successors venerated and made attempts to revive Sejong-era science and practice.{{Sfn|Lim|2019|pp=197, 205–206}} A 2024 survey by [[Gallup Korea]] of 1,777 South Koreans found that Sejong was named the second most times as their most respected historical figure, after [[Yi Sun-sin]].<ref>{{cite web |date=12 June 2024 |title= |script-title=ko:한국인이 좋아하는 50가지 [사람1편] - 역대대통령/기업인/존경하는인물/소설가/스포츠선수 (2004-2024) |trans-title=50 things Koreans love [People Part 1] - Former presidents/businessmen/respected figures/novelists/athletes (2004–2024) |url=https://www.gallup.co.kr/gallupdb/reportContent.asp?seqNo=1487 |access-date=2025-08-05 |publisher=[[Gallup Korea]] |language=ko}}</ref> Sejong's creation of the Korean alphabet is celebrated every 9 October as [[Hangul Day]], a national holiday.<ref>{{cite web|title=Oct. 9-Hangul Day: A Democratic alphabet created for Korean commoner|newspaper=[[Stars and Stripes (newspaper)|Stars and Stripes]]|url=https://korea.stripes.com/travel/oct-9-hangul-day-a-democratic-alphabet-created-for-korean-commoner.html|last1=Kim|first1=Chihon|date=27 September 2023}}</ref>

Multiple places in South Korea, including [[Sejongno|Sejong Street]],<ref name="tourguide">{{cite web |title=Tour Guide |url=http://www.tourguide.co.kr/local/local_detail.htm?pCode=CULTTOMB0262 |access-date=2016-02-22 |website=Tourguide.vo.kr}}</ref> [[Sejong–Pocheon Expressway]], and [[Sejong City]], South Korea's ''de facto'' administrative capital, are named after him. Various institutes such as [[King Sejong Station]], the [[King Sejong Institute]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chang |first=Dong-woo |date=2017-12-18 |title=(Yonhap Interview) King Sejong Institute seeks more overseas branches |url=https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20171218005600315 |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=[[Yonhap News Agency]] |language=en}}</ref> the [[Sejong Center|Sejong Center for the Performing Arts]],<ref name ="tourguide" /> [[Sejong Science High School]], and [[Sejong University]] also bear his name. In North Korea, Sejong is discussed much less than in the South and more pessimistically than elsewhere.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1996-05-13 |script-title=ko:세종대왕 치적·신상 이례적 상세히 소개(평양 요즈음) |trans-title=An unusually detailed introduction of Sejong's achievements and life (Pyongyang these days) |url=https://www.hankookilbo.com/News/Read/199605130025364846 |access-date=2025-08-05 |work=[[Hankook Ilbo]] |language=ko}}</ref> According to South Korean researcher of North Korea Lee Kyu-Duk, one North Korean history book ''Chosŏn t'ongsa'' ({{Korean|hangul=조선통사|labels=no}}) claims that Hangul was invented in order to facilitate feudal exploitation of the peasantry. While the book evaluates Hangul's linguistic features positively, it downplays the contributions of Sejong in developing the script and instead attributes its development to the intellect of the masses.<ref name="NK Sejong">{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=Kyu-Duk |date=2000 |script-title=ko:북한주민이 존경하는 민족사의 인물 |trans-title=Cultural heroes that North Koreans admire |url=https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART001367438 |journal=통일정책연구 |language=ko |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=8–9 |via=[[Korea Citation Index]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> Lee argued the following quote from a North Korean history work was representative of North Korean writings on Sejong:{{Blockquote|text=During his 30-year reign, Sejong played a major role in repelling foreign invasions, reclaiming the old territories of Goguryeo and Balhae, and developing feudal culture. However, as the monarch of a feudal state, everything he did was in service of consolidating feudalism. Thus, even during his reign, which was dubbed "an era of peace", peasant uprisings against feudal oppression and exploitation occurred several times.<ref name="NK Sejong" />|source=''Chosŏn ryŏksa sangsik'' ({{Korean|hangul=조선력사상식|labels=no}})}}
